newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Slough boosts hopes of UK property upturn.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Slough boosts hopes of UK property upturn.

text.p: A rash of positive broker reports and a strong set of results from Slough Estates Plc on Thursday have raised hopes that Britain's febrile property sector may be on the verge of a sustained upswing.

Slough, owner of a string of industrial, office and retail properties, provided concrete evidence of the upturn with growth in rental income helping fuel a 14 percent jump in half-year pre-tax profit to 37.4 million pounds ($58.33 million).
The results helped boost selected property stocks, with British Land up 7.5 pence at 467 and Hammerson Plc up 3 1/2 at 386 following hard on the heels of Slough, whose shares added 13 1/2 to 249.
Slough executive chairman Sir Nigel Mobbs told Reuters that the recovery underway is very different to the unsustainable boom conditions of the 1980s.

"What we're seeing this time is that the improvement is being driven by genuine occupancy interest whereas in the 1980s it was being driven by investment interest: this is a much healthier system," he added.
The property business was given a further vote of confidence on Thursday when investment bank Merrill Lynch told Reuters that "on a technical basis it is our most favored sector."

And rival SBC Warburg added that most of its predictions for the U.K. property sector in 1995 are on course, including a forecast of five percent growth in rental incomes, although it shaved down its forecast on capital growth to five percent from six percent.

SBC Warburg said Britain is far from witnessing the kind of property boom seen between 1986 and 1989, when rents soared to record levels and vacancy rates in central London offices slipped as low as two percent. But it said there were tentative signs that British institutions may be looking at investing in property directly for the first time in 2 1/2 years.

One of the first to put its toe in the water recently was pension and life insurance group Standard Life, which spent 40 million pounds acquiring the landmark Tower Records building in London's Piccadilly Circus.
"U.K. institutions seem to be looking at direct property assets as a viable asset class," SBC Warburg said.
Analysts point to the fact that property investment shares, which traditionally trade at a discount to net asset value, are now close to trading at a premium.

The last time this happened was in the mini-boom of late 1993 and early 1994 when stocks stood at a 20 percent premium to net asset value. But when rental growth failed to match expectations, the bubble burst.
However, a strong note of scepticism was injected by Paul Ives of the independent Applied Property Research (APR).

Ives warned a speculative construction boom is currently under way in London's office sector, with commercial construction starts in the capital up by 50 percent from a year ago, which is not being matched in the rest of Britain, or by demand.
"There is a leap of faith that demand will come along later," Ives said.
